customer_question: If our RF test result doesn't come out clean, what verification steps should we run before concluding it's a real failure?
question_variants: What should we check before treating an inconsistent RF result as a true failure?
Could a loose antenna/module connector be causing our RF test result?
What retest sequence rules out a connector issue versus a real RF problem?
actual_issue: An RF test result on a test sample was uncertain/did not go smoothly, and it needed to be determined whether this reflected a genuine RF non-compliance or a physical connection issue (a loose or improperly seated module-to-housing RF connector) before reporting a result to the customer.
plain_english_explanation: When an RF test doesn't pass cleanly, it's not always because the product itself has a real radio problem -- sometimes it's just a loose connector inside the test sample. Before treating the result as a genuine failure, the consultant has the customer physically reseat the connector a couple of times and rerun a couple of specific RF checks to confirm the connection is good, and only then proceeds to the more detailed radio test.
consultant_answer: Before the Profile test, run this verification sequence on the test unit: (1) per the customer's own request, open the test sample's housing cover, disconnect and reconnect the module's uFL connector two to three times, then close the housing back up; (2) run the relevant RF receiver and transmitter test items and confirm they pass, which the consultant noted is likely just re-confirming the RF connector connection already addressed in step (1); (3) proceed with the RF PHY test procedure, clearing the chipset vendor's app log first, run the relevant RF PHY receiver item, and capture both the InterLab test log and the chipset vendor app's log. In a later message, the consultant clarified that step (2) has little independent value and can be skipped, going directly from the connector reseat in step (1) to the RF PHY step (3).
decision_logic: An inconsistent or failing RF result should not be reported to the customer as a genuine non-compliance until a physical connector-seating explanation has been ruled out via a defined reseat-and-retest protocol; once that is done, the items confirming basic RF receive/transmit function add little additional information and the streamlined path is to go straight from the connector check to the RF PHY differential test.
final_recommendation: When an RF result is uncertain, first reseat the relevant RF connector two to three times and rerun only the RF PHY differential step (clearing the vendor app log first and capturing both InterLab and vendor app logs); skip the intermediate RF receive/transmit confirmation step as low-value.
risk_if_done_wrong: Skipping the connector-reseat check and treating the result as a genuine RF failure risks reporting an incorrect failure to the customer and triggering unnecessary investigation or re-testing of a problem that was actually a loose connector.
